#**Background**
Algorithms are playing an increasingly vital role in medical devices.   Understanding the impact of curating accessible datasets on algorithm development and evaluation, the FDA collaborated with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and Johns Hopkins School of Medicine to establish this open-access dataset containing raw (unprocessed) inertial measurement unit (IMU) and sensorized insole data from 100 individuals with Parkinson’s Disease (PD) and 85 age-matched controls synchronized to a gait reference system. Frame-by-frame annotation of participant actions during gait and balance tasks was incorporated into the dataset using video cameras synchronized to all systems. To expand the utility of this dataset, all data are associated with demographic information and clinical evaluations (e.g., medications, DBS-status, MDS-UPDRS scores). This wearables dataset can serve as a tool to assess novel algorithms for deriving gait metrics through wearables, establish distributions and variability of wearable-derived gait metrics, and provide correlational information about clinical evaluations and wearable-derived gait metrics, among other things.

In addition to the cross-sectional dataset, a longitudinal subset has been collected in which a group of participants with Parkinson’s disease (n = 47) returned for repeat assessments using the same protocol. These longitudinal data enable investigation of within-subject variability and progression over time.

This wiki brings together in a hyperlinked format everything needed to work with these data, including: description of the data collection procedures, data processing and alignment, annotation processes, and data quality control processes.

Explore the links below for additional details regarding the data and processing approaches, how to access the data, publications using these data, and contact information.

About the Catalog of Regulatory Science Tools
The enclosed tool is part of the Catalog of Regulatory Science Tools, which provides a peer- reviewed resource for stakeholders to use where standards and qualified Medical Device Development Tools (MDDTs) do not yet exist. These tools do not replace FDA-recognized standards or MDDTs. This catalog collates a variety of regulatory science tools that the FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health's (CDRH) Office of Science and Engineering Labs (OSEL) developed. These tools use the most innovative science to support medical device development and patient access to safe and effective medical devices.
